big_idea: Counting FORWARD makes amounts BIGGER; counting BACKWARD makes them SMALLER. Direction tells us.
learning_intention: We are learning that counting forward makes the amount bigger and counting backward makes the amount smaller, and we are using our feet on the Counting Path to feel the change.
student_learning_goal: I can count forward and backward and tell what happens to the amount.
success_criteria: I can step forward on the Counting Path and say each number out loud (0, 1, 2, 3 …).
I can step backward on the Counting Path and say each number out loud (5, 4, 3, 2 …).
I can tell my partner whether the amount got BIGGER or SMALLER after I stepped.
lesson_specific_materials: Counting Path floor mat (numbered 0–20 with footprints), unrolled in an open carpet area
A small stack of linking cubes (about 10) per partner pair
One small basket of paper apples (M5) for the recess countdown demo
Two arrow cards: a green FORWARD arrow and a red BACKWARD arrow, large enough to hold up at the carpet
A snack-time timer or kitchen timer for the 'countdown to recess' moment
Anchor chart paper labelled 'FORWARD = BIGGER · BACKWARD = SMALLER' with two columns

minds_on.hook: Mae and Theo are baking apple muffins, but they keep peeking at the timer because RECESS is coming. Today the Counting Crew will teach us a special chef trick: counting BACKWARD when we are waiting for something exciting.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Mae and Theo. 'Friends, Mae and Theo started baking muffins twelve minutes ago. They keep asking — how long until recess?' Hold up five paper apples in a basket. 'Yesterday we counted UP — one apple, two apples, three apples — to find HOW MANY. The amount got BIGGER each time. Watch.'

 Add an apple as you count: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. 'Forward counting makes the amount BIGGER.' Hold up the green FORWARD arrow. Now take an apple OUT of the basket. 'But what if we are waiting? Like waiting for recess? Then we count BACKWARD. Five … four … three … two … one … RECESS!' Take an apple out on each number. The basket empties. 'Backward counting makes the amount SMALLER.' Hold up the red BACKWARD arrow. 'Today on the Counting Path, your feet will feel the difference.'

Counting Crew refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'FORWARD grows it BIGGER — BACKWARD shrinks it SMALLER! That's the Counting Crew job!'
student_actions: Watch Mae and Theo set up the apple basket.
Count along 1-2-3-4-5 as the teacher adds apples (forward).
Count along 5-4-3-2-1 as the teacher takes apples out (backward).
Point to the green or red arrow when the teacher asks 'which direction?'.

action.activity_name: The Counting Path — Forward and Back

steps.instruction: Whole group at the Counting Path. The teacher demonstrates: stand on 0, then step forward one footprint at a time, calling out each number — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Hold up a small tower of cubes; add one cube on each step so children see the amount grow. Stop on 5 and ask: 'Did the cubes get bigger or smaller?' Children chorus 'BIGGER'. Then turn around and step BACKWARD from 5 to 0, removing a cube on each step. Stop on 0. 'Did the cubes get bigger or smaller?' Children chorus 'SMALLER'.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Watch my feet. When I step toward the green arrow, I'm counting FORWARD — and look, my cube tower is getting bigger and bigger. When I step toward the red arrow, I'm counting BACKWARD — and my tower is getting smaller and smaller. The DIRECTION my feet go tells us what happens to the amount.'

steps.instruction: Partner pairs take the Counting Path two at a time (others watch and chant). Partner A walks forward from 0 to 5 with a cube tower, building it up. Partner B walks backward from 5 to 0 with the same tower, taking cubes off. After each pair finishes, the watchers shout out 'BIGGER!' (forward) and 'SMALLER!' (backward) so the language sticks. Rotate every 90 seconds; aim for every child to take both directions at least once.
steps.teacher_prompt: Coach as needed: 'Slow your feet down — say the number on every footprint, not in between. If you skip a number, the cubes will skip too.' For a child who steps but stays silent, say the number with them: 'Together: ONE … TWO … THREE.'

steps.instruction: Mid-Action twist: 'mystery start'. Teacher places a child on a footprint that is NOT 0 (e.g., 7) and points at either the green or red arrow. The child has to step the right way and call out the next three numbers (e.g., starts at 7, green arrow → 8, 9, 10). This forces children to count from any starting point, not just from zero, and matches the A6.2 expectation that the SEQUENCE works in both directions everywhere on the line.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'You don't always start at zero. You might start in the middle. Watch my arrow — green or red? Tell me your three next numbers BEFORE your feet move, then walk it.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Emerging children stay in the 0-to-5 range and walk with a stronger partner who narrates each number. The teacher physically taps each footprint as the child steps. Skip the 'mystery start' twist — finish the lesson on the basic forward-then-backward demonstration only.
differentiation.for_extending: Extending children walk all the way to 10 (or 20 if confident). They also do 'skip-counting' demos by 2s on the path (0, 2, 4 …) and tell the class whether their cubes are still going BIGGER or SMALLER each time. Some can predict: 'If I'm on 8 and step FORWARD twice, where will I be?' before walking it.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Pre-teach the four target words with hand gestures: FORWARD (open hand pushing away from chest), BACKWARD (open hand pulling toward chest), BIGGER (hands wide apart), SMALLER (hands close together). Children echo the gesture every time the word is spoken. Provide a number line with arrows printed on the desk so they can finger-trace before foot-walking.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-PURCHASE PATH: skip the printed Counting Path mat and cube towers entirely. Bodies become the path — line up 11 children in a row (each is one number 0-10); a 'walker' steps in front of each child saying their number; the 'walker' starts at one end and walks forward (FORWARD chant), then back (BACKWARD chant); the LINED-UP children make their bodies BIGGER (arms wide overhead) when called forward and SMALLER (arms tucked low) when called backward. Whole lesson runs on bodies, voice, and gestures — no purchased mat, no cubes.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: (a) does the child say each number aloud as they step, or do they skip / stay silent? (b) does the child move feet in the direction the teacher's arrow points (green = forward, red = backward), or do they default to forward regardless? (c) when prompted 'is the amount BIGGER or SMALLER now?', does the child use the matched word, or stick to one word for both directions? Children who match the direction word to the arrow are secure on A6.2.
formative_check.how_to_record: Class formative checklist with rows for each child and three columns: 'narrates each number', 'matches feet to arrow', 'uses bigger/smaller correctly'. Tick during the partner walks; circle gaps for tomorrow's small-group recovery.

consolidation.activity_name: Bigger or Smaller? Counting Crew Conversation
discussion_prompts: Mae just asked us — when she counts the muffins coming OUT of the oven, is that forward or backward? Why?
Theo wants to know — if our timer says 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 … what is happening to the time we have left?
Show me with your hands: was it BIGGER or SMALLER when you walked toward the red arrow on the Counting Path?
consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. s the Counting Crew job!' Then each child names ONE direction word (forward or backward) and ONE size word (bigger or smaller) that go together. The teacher tallies pairings on the anchor chart. By the end the chart should clearly show FORWARD pairs with BIGGER and BACKWARD pairs with SMALLER.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Per-child formative checklist with three indicators recorded during the partner walks (narrates each number, matches feet to arrow, uses the correct size word). Anchor-chart tally from the exit routine showing how cleanly the class paired FORWARD with BIGGER and BACKWARD with SMALLER. Photo of the Counting Path with each child's name written on the highest footprint they reached.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: A6.2 'understand when counting forward, the quantity gets bigger and when counting backward, the quantity gets smaller' is a directional concept — children must connect a SEQUENCE direction to a SIZE change. The formative tier is appropriate here because the unit will revisit bidirectional counting in Lesson 4 (subitizing) and Lesson 5 (composing/decomposing); this lesson establishes the bigger/smaller language that those later lessons depend on.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the Child Steps Backward but Says 'Bigger' — repairing the direction-to-size link (Fuson, 1988 Number Word Sequence; Sarama & Clements, 2009)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A6.2 directional counting, the most-documented K trap is for a child to walk the right direction but use the wrong size word. They've learned that COUNTING means BIGGER (from Lesson 1 and from years of being asked 'how many?'), so when they count 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 backward, the COUNTING habit overrides the BACKWARD direction and they still say 'bigger'.

Fuson's (1988) Number Word Sequence (NWS) framework traces children's progressive mastery: string-level (the count words are an undifferentiated chant — 'onetwothreefourfive'), unbreakable-list-level (countable but only from 1), breakable-chain-level (can resume from any number forward), numerable-chain-level (can count forward AND backward, can count up-to and count-down-to with bidirectional fluency). Backward counting is one full level past forward fluency — children who can rote-count to 30 forward may still be at the unbreakable-list stage and panic when asked to count down from 5. The 'mystery start' twist (Step 3) is engineered to surface NWS string-level freezes.

Sarama & Clements (2009) place direction-quantity coordination explicitly in their counting trajectory: forward-counts-bigger and backward-counts-smaller is a SEPARATE level from rote bidirectional sequencing. A child can recite 5-4-3-2-1 from memory and STILL not connect that recitation to a shrinking quantity — exactly the trap this lesson catches. The cube tower is the empirical bridge: the SHRINKING tower in their hand makes the size-direction link physical.

Why this matters: K children who exit with the size-direction link missing arrive in Grade 1 unable to use number-line subtraction or count-down strategies for take-away problems. The repair must happen at K with embodied counter-evidence.

Step 2 (partner walks) is where the teacher catches this. The script below covers exactly what to say when a child walks backward but uses the wrong size word, and why the cube tower is the recovery tool.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Counting Path is unrolled. The pair has just finished — Partner B walked from 5 back to 0 with a cube tower, taking cubes off on each step. The tower started at five cubes and is now down to one (or zero). Partner B is standing on footprint 0 holding the small tower. Teacher steps in BEFORE the next pair starts.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script: Crouch beside Partner B. Hold up their tower next to where it started (five cubes high) — visualise the SHRINK with your hands. 'Tell me what happened to your cube tower when you walked backward.' If they say 'bigger', stay calm — this is the teaching moment. 'Hmm, let us look together. When you started, how many cubes did you have?' Hold up five fingers. 'And when you finished?' Hold up zero or one finger. 'So — did the tower get bigger, or smaller?' Wait. They will usually self-correct: 'smaller'. Affirm: 'YES — smaller. When your feet went BACKWARD, the cubes got SMALLER. Now let us say it together: BACKWARD makes the amount … SMALLER.' Have them echo with the hand gestures (hands closing in for SMALLER). Walk them through one more backward step, this time narrating with them: 'feet going backward … cubes going smaller'. If they STILL say 'bigger' even after the cube demo, it's not a misconception about direction — it's a habit-driven word slip. Move them to the green arrow side and have them count forward 0 to 3, then ask 'bigger or smaller?' (correct: bigger). Then send them backward 3 to 0, and ask again. The contrast between adjacent forward and backward walks usually breaks the habit. Tick the 'uses bigger/smaller correctly' column once they nail the contrast, even if it took two attempts. Note in the comments column: 'needed cube re-show' — that's a flag to give them a one-on-one bigger/smaller round at tomorrow's morning meeting before Lesson 3.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Walks backward but still says 'bigger' — the counting habit overrides the direction. Most common K starting point.
(Mid) Says 'smaller' once you point at the cube tower, but defaults to 'bigger' again on the next backward walk without prompting.
(Strong) On the second backward walk, says 'smaller' before the cubes are even removed, because they've internalised the direction-to-size link.
(Stretched) Volunteers a real-life example: 'Like when there's only ONE muffin left — that's smaller than five muffins.' Generalises beyond the path.
common_misconceptions: Counting always makes the amount bigger. (Child has only ever counted up, so counting and growing are the same word in their head. Most common K starting point.)
The numbers on the Counting Path are 'just labels' — stepping on 5 doesn't mean five of anything. (Child can recite 0-20 but does not connect each number to a quantity. The cube tower is the repair.)
Backward = wrong. (Some children believe counting backward is a mistake — they self-correct mid-walk and start over from 0. Affirm that backward IS counting, just in a different direction.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child walks backward but says 'bigger' (counting-equals-bigger habit slip): use the cube tower every time. Words alone don't repair this — child must SEE the tower shrink in their hands while their feet step backward. Hold the tower NEXT TO their starting height (5) and ending height (0-1) for visual contrast. Embodiment, not explanation.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child can chant 5-4-3-2-1 from memory but freezes at the 'mystery start' from a non-zero non-five footprint (NWS string-level freeze, Fuson 1988): walk WITH the child, footprint by footprint, narrating the next number each time their foot lands. Build the breakable chain experientially before re-asking them to predict. Repeat with 3 different mystery starts before retesting independence.

DIAGNOSTIC C — child treats backward counting as a mistake (starts over from 0 or refuses to count down): explicitly affirm that backward IS counting; pair adjacent forward-then-backward walks so the child experiences both directions as legitimate; cite the recess countdown ('5, 4, 3, 2, 1 — RECESS!') as a real-life backward count they ALREADY know works. Do not let the child finish the lesson with 'backward = wrong' framing intact.

worksheet_brief.worksheet_title: My Counting Path: Big or Small
worksheet_brief.purpose: End-of-lesson consolidation. Children draw and label a short Counting Path of their own, then circle whether the amount got BIGGER or SMALLER for each direction. Captures formative-level evidence for A6.2 and reinforces the direction-to-size pairing established on the floor mat. Goes home as a take-home explainer ('Show your family how the Counting Crew counts forward and backward').

parts_outline.task: Trace the green arrow and count forward: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Circle: did the amount get BIGGER or SMALLER?
Trace the red arrow and count backward: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0. Circle: did the amount get BIGGER or SMALLER?
Draw three muffins on the tray. Then draw the tray after Mae takes one muffin away. Was that counting forward or backward?
